tier_reason: Author's own blog shows a 'CLI ROW COUNTING PERFORMANCE (1M rows)' table (miller 0.004s, cisv 0.055s, wc -l 0.083s, rust-csv 0.664s, csvkit 9.788s) and Node.js sync throughput (cisv 60.80 MB/s vs papaparse 25.12 MB/s); compiler flags are given but no CPU model, so first-party partial methodology = C.

corrections.workload: Row counting on a 1M-row (98MB) CSV via CLI, wall-clock time vs miller, wc -l, rust-csv and csvkit (xsv is named in the methodology but absent from the results table); also Node.js synchronous parse throughput vs PapaParse/csv-parse
corrections.claimed_speedup: ~178x faster than csvkit on 1M-row row counting (9.788s vs 0.055s; derived from page data); ~2.4x faster than PapaParse in Node.js sync mode (60.80 MB/s vs 25.12 MB/s; derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: Repo is archived by its own author. CPU model not stated (compiler flags -O3 -march=native -mavx512f -mavx512bw given, hardware not), so evidence stops short of Tier A/B. The CLI test is row counting, not full parsing; the 178x is against csvkit (a Python tool), while miller is faster than cisv in the same table (0.004s) and cisv is only slightly faster than wc -l. Author notes the code evolved during the article so numbers may not match the current code.

notes: Numbers match the page; workload corrected from 'parsing' to 'row counting' and derived marker added to the PapaParse ratio. Archived, 91 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-03-05 confirmed.

tier_reason: Third-party blog (duckdblab.org, which calls itself an independent blog, not DuckDB Labs) shows pd.read_csv + groupby vs DuckDB SQL over access_log.csv: ~3.8s vs ~180s (47x), ~380MB vs ~4.2GB, on Ryzen 9 7950X; no benchmark script and not a well-known suite, so C.

corrections.caveats: Published on duckdblab.org, which calls itself an 'Independent DuckDB Technical Blog' not affiliated with DuckDB Labs, not on duckdb.org or a well-known benchmark suite. No linked benchmark script; the workload is introduced as 'Assume we have a real Nginx access log access_log.csv'; versions loosely specified ('DuckDB v1.5.x' plus some v2.0 Preview features); author says 'results may vary by machine'. The pandas baseline is a naive full pd.read_csv load with no chunking or dtype tuning, and a ~4.2GB pandas footprint for an 8GB CSV looks low, so treat the numbers cautiously.

notes: Numbers and hardware match the page. I replaced the caveat that called 47x 'above the 50x threshold' (it is below). The source is weak (an unaffiliated blog with a hypothetical framing), so a stronger first-party or independent DuckDB-vs-pandas CSV source would be better if enrichment finds one.

tier_reason: Official Polars blog, 'CSV writer speed up' section: 'The latest Polars version is ~45x times faster than pandas and ~3.5x faster than pyarrow', plus 0.20.30 8.975s vs 0.20.19 14.684s on a MacBook Pro M3 24GB; no benchmark code or build flags, so first-party C.

corrections.caveats: First-party official blog post. The M3 hardware sentence opens the same CSV-writer benchmark section as the pandas/pyarrow relative-speedup plots, but the post does not say outright that the 45x figure comes from the same run. No benchmark code or build flags are given, and the pandas/pyarrow ratios come from plots, with no absolute times for those libraries. This is a CSV write benchmark (Parquet read + CSV write), not CSV read.

notes: All quoted numbers are verbatim on the page. MIT, 39,859 stars and a last commit of 2026-09-25 are confirmed. The record's mention of independent 2-16x CSV read benchmarks was not checked.

tier_reason: Maintainer jqnatividad's discussion (2022-04-28): 'pandas took 12 seconds to calculate statistics qsv computed in less than 0.16 seconds (75x faster) for a 124MB, 2.7M row CSV file', with --everything taking 2s (6x). No hardware for that figure and no code, and >50x with unstated flags, so C.

corrections.caveats: The numbers come from the qsv maintainer in a GitHub Discussion (2022-04-28), not a blog post or paper, so they reflect a 2022-era qsv. Hardware and compiler flags are not given for the 75x figure (its footnote only cites the qsv whirlwind tour), and the ratio is above 50x, so the tier is capped at C. The Ryzen 7 4800H / 32GB footnote belongs to a separate 22.4s NYC-311 run (27.8M rows, 16GB) with no pandas comparison. qsv began as a fork of BurntSushi/xsv but GitHub no longer tracks it as a fork. GitHub reports the license as NOASSERTION, but LICENSE-MIT and COPYING say qsv is MIT-only after v21.1.1 (v21.1.1 and earlier were also under the Unlicense).

notes: Numbers are verbatim on the page. License confirmed as MIT from LICENSE-MIT, COPYING and Cargo.toml despite gh's NOASSERTION; 3,796 stars and a last commit of 2026-09-25 are confirmed.

tier_reason: Tidyverse blog table on the 1.55GB, 14.7M-row, 11-column taxi data: base R read.delim reads in 1m 21.5s (1m 22.6s total) vs vroom 3.6s (7s total); no CPU or flags. The linked benchmark vignette adds public code (inst/bench/taxi) and an EC2 m5.4xlarge but no compiler or flags, so first-party C.

corrections.workload: Reading a 1.55GB / 14.7M-row / 11-column real-world taxi-trip CSV and running read+print+head+tail+sample+filter+summarise, vroom vs base R read.delim (also readr and data.table)
corrections.claimed_speedup: ~22.6x faster on initial read alone (1m 21.5s vs 3.6s; derived from page data); ~11.8x faster for the full workflow (1m 22.6s vs 7s; derived from page data)
corrections.caveats: The baseline is base R's read.delim (the post's table row), not read.csv; it is a widely used incumbent in another language ecosystem. The 2019 blog gives no hardware or build flags. The updated benchmark vignette (vroom 1.5.1, 2021-06-22, EC2 m5.4xlarge with 16 vCPUs, code in inst/bench/taxi) shows read.delim 1m 12.3s read vs vroom 1.3s read (1m 14.5s vs 6.7s total with dplyr+Altrep), but still no compiler or flags. vroom's read time relies partly on lazy Altrep materialization, which shifts cost to later filter and summarise steps.

notes: Baseline corrected from read.csv to read.delim, as the page shows. The last commit on the default branch (main) is 2026-06-09; 2026-09-21 is only pushed_at. License is MIT per DESCRIPTION ('MIT + file LICENSE') and LICENSE.md despite gh's NOASSERTION; status is still active.
